I wait. I do not move. I barely breathe. I watch Mama's face—Freya, I mean, Freya Hartigan with her government papers and pretending not to be scared of the dark either—and I decide in this waiting whether anyone heard me at all.

No—no, I know Mama heard. She always hears. That's the unfair part of her. She hears and doesn't always answer, which is different from not-listening, and I am old enough to know the difference. Three years, three whole years, and I know the difference. I want to say again—wait wait wait, I have more to say about the chores, about how I stacked the blocks from biggest to smallest and even the blue one that doesn't fit right because someone bit it—I want to say again but I press my lips together. I learned that: pressing. I learned it from the time I told Odette's secret about the crayon and the wall, and everyone was angry at me for knowing when I shouldn't have. I can spot a lie fast. Faster than them. But I don't always know when to press my lips until it's done and then it's done.

The stairs creak. Someone is always on the stairs. Maybe Petra coming back from the forest, smelling like outside. I want to go outside. Past the farmland. Wren Thorne talks about beyond like it's something you can point to, like "the kitchen" or "the dark under the stairs," but when I ask where exactly he just laughs. Adults laugh when children ask where exactly and it makes me suspicious. I am suspicious of Wren Thorne. But I still want to know.

I look at Odette. She breathes loud. I could tell her that. I could tell her right now. But it's a secret, kind of, how loud she breathes, and I keep secrets. I do. I keep them and I stack them like blocks, biggest to smallest, and I wait until someone asks exactly the right way.

The election. Mama said something about the election yesterday when she thought I was napping. Empty seats. Someone has to sit in them or everyone falls down, I think. Like a chair. Like when I pulled out Freya's chair as a joke and she almost fell and no one laughed, not even me after. Seats are serious. Authority comes from the crowd, not the office—that's what I know, no one taught me, I just know it—but someone still has to sit there or the desk gets dusty and no one knows what to do about the tax.

I want to declare. I want to stand at the town hall and say "I, Wendell Hartigan, am three, and I do chores without being asked." I want to see if they'd let me. If the crowd would let me. But the farmland first. The edge. The question of beyond.

Mama still hasn't answered. Odette is awake now, pretending not to be, I can tell by her blinking. I can always tell. I'm very good at telling. Everyone should know.

I will wait one more minute, and then I will ask again about the farmland, but softer this time, because loud hasn't worked yet and I have been burned once and never forget it.
